Hung by Design: Malaysia's Three-Way Tie and the Bargaining After GE16

  1. 29 Oct 2026 · @Sam

Summary

  1. Malaysia's 16th general election ended in a three-way tie (PH 62, PN 62, BN 60 of 222 seats). Specific groups of voters made it happen, and a handful of leaders will now decide what it produces.

What voters did

  1. Malay voters who backed PN in 2022 as a protest split three ways. Some stayed with PAS in the north and east coast, and others returned to UMNO in Pahang, Perak, Johor and Melaka, which let BN win mixed Malay-majority seats it lost in 2022.
  2. Non-Malay voters stayed with PH, but fewer turned out in marginal seats. That kept PH's urban core intact while costing it about 20 seats in Selangor, Negeri Sembilan and Johor.
  3. Chinese and Indian voters in mixed seats backed MCA and MIC candidates on top of BN's Malay base. Those votes gave BN the plurality it needed to turn about 28% of the vote into 60 seats.
  4. Urban and suburban Malay voters moved away from Bersatu. Its narrow 2022 wins in Pahang and Perak were the first to flip back to BN, which cut its tally and left PAS as the dominant partner in PN.

What leaders are likely to do

  1. Anwar Ibrahim will claim the first attempt at a government on PH's lead in vote share, and will offer UMNO posts and seat arrangements to keep it from PAS, while resisting any public concession on prosecutions.
  2. Ahmad Zahid Hamidi will negotiate with PH and PN at the same time and delay, because either choice splits UMNO, and he will present the final decision as forced by the "fresh mandate" argument he has already made.
  3. Abdul Hadi Awang will push an UMNO-PAS partnership and trade the premiership for state autonomy and the religious and education portfolios, while refusing seat deals that cost PAS seats it already holds.
  4. Muhyiddin Yassin will threaten separate talks with PH or UMNO, since Bersatu's 20 seats are his only leverage and PAS leads PN.
  5. Abang Johari Openg and Hajiji Noor will wait until BN has chosen, then back whichever grouping offers Borneo the most devolution, and defer formally to the Agong.
  6. BN's ability to join either rival is what gives it leverage over a result in which it took the smallest share of the vote. Which of the three deals forms depends mainly on whether Zahid can hold UMNO's divided base, whether Hadi accepts being the junior partner, and whether Muhyiddin defects.

The result: three blocs within two seats of each other

  1. The blocs finished within two seats of one another even though BN took the smallest vote share, so the outcome was driven by how votes were distributed, not by how many were cast. Against GE15 (PH 82, PN 74, BN 30), BN gained 30 seats while PH lost 20 and PN lost 12, so BN's gain came from both rivals at once. Two features of the geography explain it. BN's support sits in mixed Malay-majority seats, where a plurality wins on a split vote. PH's non-Malay vote is concentrated in urban seats, where it produces very large majorities that count no more than a one-vote win.
  1. The change in each major party's seats against GE15 shows which voters moved:
  1. UMNO's gain of 26 is close to the combined loss of PAS, Bersatu, DAP and PKR (30), which is the signature of a Malay-vote recovery, not a general swing. DAP and PKR lost equally, which points to Malay-minority marginals and turnout, not a collapse in non-Malay support. PAS lost the least relative to its base, because its heartland seats are the hardest to flip.
  2. The 112-seat threshold turns this distribution into a bargaining problem. A bloc plus Borneo and the smaller seats reaches only about 100, so a government needs two of the three big blocs or a split of one. Because PH and PN are the least compatible pair, BN sits in almost every credible majority.

Why the vote split this way

  1. The tie came from four groups of voters making different choices from those they made in 2022, and from one structural feature that made all four choices push seats the same way. At GE15 about 57% of peninsular Malay voters backed PN and more than 80% of non-Malay voters backed PH, so any large shift had to come from the Malay electorate or from turnout.
  2. 1. Malay protest voters split. These voters chose PN in 2022 mainly to punish UMNO and to reject a PH they saw as dependent on non-Malay support. In GE16 some stayed with PAS in the north and east coast, while others returned to UMNO in Pahang, Perak, Johor and Melaka. A protest vote has a motive that expires: after years of PN as the main opposition, with PAS's religious agenda and Bersatu-PAS friction on display, voters could punish and endorse separately. PAS's heartland seats held because there the vote was an identity choice, not a protest.
  3. 2. UMNO loyalists returned once UMNO looked viable. At GE15 UMNO's peninsular seats fell from 54 to 20 and its vote share from 20.9% to about 12%, with many Pahang and Perak losses narrow. These voters had no comparable alternative in 2022, since PN offered an ideological break and PH was unacceptable, so they stayed home or defected without conviction. By GE16 UMNO's branch networks and patronage were rebuilt enough to ask them back, which is why most of its 26-seat gain came from seats it had lost narrowly.
  4. 3. Non-Malay voters stayed with PH but turned out less where their vote did not decide the seat. DAP's vote share fell from 19.9% to about 18% and PKR's from 18.9% to about 14% at GE15, and PH already took more than 80% of non-Malay votes, so there was no upside left to mobilise. The cost fell in Malay-minority and mixed marginals in Selangor, Negeri Sembilan and Johor, where PH lost about 20 seats (DAP down 9, PKR down 9).
  5. 4. Chinese and Indian voters in mixed seats gave BN a plurality. In three-cornered contests where PH was not competitive, voters who feared PAS's influence treated BN's MCA and MIC candidates as the safer option. Because these seats are won on a plurality, those votes on top of BN's Malay base were enough to convert about 28% of the national vote into 60 seats.
  6. 5. Urban and suburban Malay voters moved away from Bersatu. Bersatu's 24 seats in 2022 came on about 11% of the vote and rested on borrowed support. When a viable BN candidate was available and PN had become PAS-led, its narrowest seats in Pahang and Perak, where PN took 17 of 41 and 26 of 59 state seats at GE15, were the first to revert. The loss of 4 seats left PAS as the dominant partner in PN.
  7. The structural feature is first-past-the-post combined with three near-equal blocs. A shift of a few percentage points in a mixed seat changes the winner without any change in overall support, and each bloc was strongest exactly where the others were weakest. Each had exhausted its natural territory in the same election, which is why none gained decisively.

The principals: who decides, and what each leader wants

  1. With no bloc near 112, the outcome turns on a handful of leaders, and their behaviour is best explained by what each stands to lose, not by ideology. The table sets out each leader's position as shown in 2026 reporting. The analysis after it is a projection from those positions, not a report of events.
  1. This brief assumes the PN pairing of PAS and Bersatu survived to polling day, despite the open rift that followed PAS's June 2026 decision to end cooperation with Bersatu.

Objectives, constraints and likely moves

Three relationships decide which deal forms.

  1. Anwar and Zahid decide whether Option 1 is possible. Zahid's leverage is the argument that Anwar's premiership rests on UMNO's support, so any exit by UMNO requires a fresh mandate. Anwar's leverage is the premiership itself, which UMNO cannot hold in a PH-led government.
  2. Zahid and Hadi decide Options 2 and 3. Their parties warmed through 2026 around Malay-Muslim unity, but they must reconcile two public positions: Hadi's pledge to defend every PAS-held seat and Mohamad Hasan's refusal to compromise on seat distribution.
  3. Muhyiddin and the PAS leadership decide whether PN stays whole. BN plus PAS reaches only 101 seats, so Bersatu's 20 are required for the BN-PN pairing in Option 2. That gives Muhyiddin leverage that his party's size would not otherwise confer, and a motive to use it before PAS and UMNO settle terms that exclude him.

Option 1: PH + BN, a unity-style government (122 seats)

  1. The arithmetic. PH (62) and BN (60) give 122 seats, so 11 MPs leaving the government's column would end the majority. Adding GPS gives 145 and adding GRS gives 151, which would take 34 and 40 defections respectively to end it. The deal is therefore safe only if Borneo joins.
  2. Why both sides want it. Each is choosing the lesser of two evils. PH's alternative is opposition, and BN's is being the junior partner to PAS. The pairing also fits the seat map: PH supplies the urban non-Malay seats that BN cannot win, and BN supplies the Malay-majority seats PH cannot win, which is the combination that formed the original 112-seat basis of the unity government.
  3. What each side trades. PH offers the premiership, which Anwar needs and which UMNO cannot hold in a PH-led government, and it wants UMNO's seats to stabilise its Malay-minority marginals. BN offers its 60 seats and wants the deputy premiership, a major economic or home portfolio, protection of Malay and Bumiputera policy, and a seat pact that stops PH challenging UMNO in mixed seats. The likely settlement gives BN more than its seat share in cabinet, narrows the reform agenda to institutional measures, and keeps the language on race policy deliberately vague.
  4. The prosecutions problem. UMNO has complained about how its leaders have been treated in prosecutions, and PH's brand rests on anti-corruption. A formula in which the Attorney-General decides cases on their merits lets Anwar describe the outcome as judicial independence and lets Zahid read it as relief, but both must preserve the ambiguity. If either states what was agreed, the other's base objects.
  5. Why it could fail. Three triggers would break it. DAP and PKR activists would revolt if the deal visibly shields UMNO leaders, and Loke's weakened position after Negeri Sembilan leaves him less able to absorb that. UMNO's PAS-friendly faction, encouraged by the unity-rally narrative, could push Zahid to defect. And a Malay backlash against the deal would favour PAS at the next election, giving UMNO an incentive to leave before then.

Option 2: BN + PN, a Malay-unity government (122 seats)

  1. The arithmetic. BN (60) and PN (62) give 122 seats, so 11 MPs leaving would end the majority, and the total is 151 with Borneo. The detail that matters is that BN plus PAS alone reaches only 101, so Bersatu's 20 seats are required. That gives Muhyiddin a veto his party's size would not otherwise confer.
  2. Why both sides want it. UMNO and PAS compete for the same rural Malay seats in the north, Pahang and Perak. In three-cornered contests they split the Malay vote and let a rival win, so sharing seats removes a cost that both bear. One formula analysed in the press makes the sharing mechanical by giving each seat to whichever party polled higher in it.
  3. What each side trades. UMNO is the larger party (53 seats against PAS's 41), so BN would claim the premiership, even though PN as a bloc has two more seats than BN (62 against 60). PAS would seek the deputy premiership, the religious affairs and education portfolios, autonomy in its northern and east-coast states, and a guarantee that BN will not contest them. MCA and MIC would need accommodation, which Hadi's openness to "non-extreme" non-Muslim partners makes easier. The likely settlement is an UMNO premier with a PAS deputy holding real authority over a named area, no new federal Islamic legislation, and a written seat formula.
  4. The seat collision. Hadi has pledged to defend every seat PAS holds, and Mohamad Hasan has said UMNO will not compromise on seat distribution. Both cannot be honoured. A vote-based formula is the likeliest way out, because each leader can claim the rule was objective. It would favour UMNO in the mixed seats of Pahang and Perak and PAS in the north, and the first test of the deal is which party ends up conceding more.
  5. Muhyiddin as spoiler. He has called the UMNO-PN alliance a realignment of power rather than genuine unity, and predicted that UMNO would eventually challenge PAS in the north. If PAS and UMNO settle terms that exclude Bersatu, he loses everything, so his incentive is to shop Bersatu's 20 seats to PH before they do. The threat is credible because the 101-seat shortfall makes it costly to ignore.
  6. Why it could fail. The main risk is the north. A seat deal that satisfies one party looks like surrender to the other, and each leader's authority depends on not appearing to concede to a historic rival. Borneo is a second risk, since reporting suggests GPS and GRS rank a PN-BN government last among their options, which gives them leverage to demand guarantees that PAS may resist.

Option 3: PAS + UMNO + Borneo, a split-bloc government (123 seats)

  1. The arithmetic. UMNO (53), PAS (41), GPS (23) and GRS (6) total 123 seats, or 117 without GRS. Only 12 defections, or 6 without GRS, would end the majority, against 34 and 40 in Options 1 and 2 once Borneo is added. The pairing excludes PH, Bersatu, MCA and MIC, so it can only form if PN splits and Bersatu is cut loose.
  2. Why it can form. For UMNO, it offers the premiership and the economic ministries without sitting with DAP or sharing Malay votes with Bersatu. For PAS, it delivers the religious and education portfolios and state autonomy, and removes Bersatu, its main rival inside PN, from the table. It is the one option in which the two largest Malay parties govern together in a way each can present to its base as Malay-Muslim unity.
  3. Why Borneo is the obstacle. Reporting on Borneo's preferences ranks a renewed deal with Anwar first, a BN-only arrangement second, and a PN-BN government a grudging third. A government that depends on PAS is therefore the least attractive to GPS and GRS, so their price would be the highest: a larger share of oil and gas revenue, devolution of education and health, implementation of Malaysia Agreement commitments, a veto over constitutional changes touching religion, language or autonomy, and a deputy prime minister's post. Abang Johari has said GPS is in no position to claim the premiership, so he would be bargaining for guarantees, not office, and Hajiji would likely follow his lead as in 2022. The settlement most likely to hold is an UMNO premier with two deputies, one from PAS and one from Sarawak, and a written understanding that PAS pursues its religious agenda at state level.
  4. The counter-coalition. An excluded Muhyiddin has every reason to bargain separately with Anwar. PH's 62 plus Bersatu's 20, GPS's 23 and GRS's 6 reaches 111, so one more seat from Warisan, Muda or the independents would tip it to 112. Option 3 would therefore compete with a PH-Bersatu-Borneo government for the same Borneo votes, and whichever offers GPS and GRS more devolution and fewer religious risks would win them.
  5. Why it could fail. The margin. With a surplus of 5 to 11 seats, three or four defections would end the government, and PH and the excluded Bersatu faction would lobby against it. The 2020 political crisis showed how quickly a thin majority can unravel. Borneo's red lines on religion would also constrain PAS from the first day.

Outlook: what to watch

  1. BN holds the strongest hand because it is the only bloc that can credibly threaten to join either rival. PH and PN cannot realistically govern together, since each would be asking its base to accept the party it spent the campaign denouncing, so BN's choice between them sets the terms. That leverage is greatest before a deal is signed and shrinks afterwards, which gives Zahid a reason to delay and to keep both channels open. The table shows where each option is weakest.
  1. Borneo is insurance in Options 1 and 2 and the pivot in Option 3. The first two clear 112 without GPS and GRS, but Borneo turns a 10-seat margin into a cushion of 30 to 40 and decides whether a government can reach the 148 seats needed for a two-thirds majority. In Option 3, Borneo supplies 29 of the 123 seats, so Abang Johari and Hajiji decide whether that government exists at all.

Signals to watch, and what each would indicate

  1. Zahid opens formal talks with PH and PN at the same time. BN is auctioning its seats, and Options 1 and 2 are both live.
  2. A joint Anwar-Zahid statement on the Attorney-General's role in prosecutions. The prosecutions problem is being solved, and Option 1 is the likely outcome.
  3. A signed Zahid-Hadi seat formula. Option 2 is forming, but only if Bersatu is kept inside PN. If Bersatu is dropped, it points to Option 3.
  4. Bersatu MPs splitting from Muhyiddin, or Muhyiddin meeting Anwar. PN is breaking, which opens Option 3 and the PH-Bersatu-Borneo counter-coalition.
  5. GPS and GRS publishing red lines on religion and autonomy before a deal. They intend to price their support in constitutional terms, which raises the cost of Option 3 the most.
  6. The wider lesson is that a three-way tie rewards the leader who is most flexible about partners and punishes the one whose base cannot tolerate the deal on offer. Each government fails when a specific group decides it has been sold out: DAP and PKR activists in Option 1, northern Malay voters in Option 2, and Borneo's electorates in Option 3. The leaders' task is to keep that group quiet long enough for the deal to deliver.
